To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cholinergic cells in the pedunculo-pontine tegmentum project to the interpolar nucleus of the trigeminal complex, and that this projection modulates the receptive fields of trigeminal neurons.

mesopontopontine cholineergic neurons project to the trigeminal interpolar nucleus where they exert a direct, powerful control over receptive fields in the first relay station of the vibrissar system.
mesopontin cholinergic neurons modulate the receptive field size of interpolaris cells, which in turn controls receptive field size in the lemnical pathway.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of cholinergic modulation on the first relay stations of a sensory system.
the role that the mesopontine tegmentum plays in the modulation of sensory information.
the study of the brainstem mechanisms that modulate the processing of tactile information in the lemniscothalamic pathway.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the mesopontine tegmentum exerts a cholinergic control over the sensory relay of vibrissal information in the lemniscl pathway, from the first relay station (interpolaris) to the last relay station (ventral posterior medial thalamic nucleus) and the primary somatosensory cortex.

cholinergic neurons in the mesopontine tegmentum exert a direct, powerful, and effective control over sensory transmission in the lemniscus pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mesopontin cholinergic neurons control sensory transmission at the very first stages of the lemniscal system in rodents.

cholinergic cells exert their action in the lemnical pathway at two levels, the spinal and interpolar nuclei, thus controlling the type of messages forwarded to the thalamic relay stations and the cerebral cortex.
cholinergic neurons are not only modulating the thalamus, but also modulating the brainstem trigeminus complex, which in turn modulates the thalamus.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cholinergically induced enhancement of sensory transmission in sensory relay nuclei is not a phenomenon restricted to the thalamocortical system, as it has been classically assumed, and that the brainstem trigeminocortical pathway is a target for cholinergic modulation as well.
the mesopontine tegmentum, in addition to its well known role in the control of the sleep-wake cycle, may also play a role in modulating sensory information in the lemniscul system.
mesopontopontine cholineergic neurons may exert a direct, modulatory control over the sensory relay in the brainstem trigeminocortical pathway.
